structure.title: Preparation
structure.text: Early chapters examine costs, calculation, and the conditions of effective action.

structure.title: Adaptation
structure.text: Later chapters turn to movement, terrain, fire, and intelligence: circumstances determine which principles can work.

people.name: The commander
people.text: The general Sun Tzu addresses, who must weigh the costs of war before it begins and is judged by victories won without wasting the army.

people.name: Deception
people.text: Sun Tzu's principle that all warfare rests on making the enemy believe what is false: appearing weak when strong, far away when near.

people.name: Terrain
people.text: The ground on which an army marches and fights, which Sun Tzu sorts into kinds, each with its own dangers and its own right way to move.

context.title: Military advice
context.text: This is a text about organised warfare. Applying its statements to business or personal relationships changes their setting and sometimes their meaning.
context.takeaway: Start with the military problem being addressed.

context.title: Compressed instruction
context.text: Short maxims can look contradictory because they address different circumstances. The commander must judge when each applies.
context.takeaway: Advice is conditional on the situation.

notice.why: Victory can become ruinous before a battle is lost.

notice.text: Notice the priority given to information.
notice.why: Knowledge can change what force is necessary.

opening: An army can win its battles and ruin the country that pays for them. Sun Tzu starts from the cost of fighting: exhausted soldiers, emptied stores, and decisions that become harder to reverse with every mile. His commander must understand terrain, deception, morale, and the enemy well enough to avoid depending on courage alone. These spare instructions give intelligence a ruthless practical purpose. The finest victory leaves little for a heroic story because the opponent's position has collapsed before the fighting begins.
